title: Network Devices & Topologies
summary: Know what hubs, switches, routers, and gateways actually do at each layer, and how the basic wiring topologies trade off failure isolation for cost.

slides.sectionTitle: The physical devices behind a network
slides.markdown: Every network is a mix of a few device types — hubs, switches, routers — each operating at a different layer, wired into some physical shape (topology). Knowing which device does what, and why star topology won, resolves most of the "what's the difference between X and Y" confusion in networking.

| Device | Layer | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Hub | Physical (1) | Repeats every incoming bit out every other port — no addressing awareness |
| Switch | Data Link (2) | Reads MAC addresses, forwards frames only to the port that needs them |
| Router | Network (3) | Reads IP addresses, forwards packets between different networks |

**How to decide which term to use:** if it's making a decision based on an address, name the layer that address belongs to — a switch decides on MAC, a router decides on IP. Hubs make no decision at all, which is exactly why they're obsolete.

slides.sectionTitle: How a switch learns and forwards
slides.markdown:
A switch starts with an empty **MAC address table**. When a frame arrives, it records "source MAC seen on this port," then checks whether it already knows the destination MAC:

- **Known** — forward only out that one port.
- **Unknown** — flood out every port except the one it arrived on, then learn the reply's source to fill in the table.

After a few frames, the switch knows every device's port and stops flooding — this **learning + forwarding** loop is why switches vastly outperform hubs on busy networks.

A router looks at a packet's **destination IP address**, consults its routing table for the best-matching entry, and forwards the packet out the corresponding interface toward the next hop — repeating this at every router along the path.

Unlike a switch's flat MAC table, a router's table is organized by **network prefixes** (covered in depth in the Routing group), which is what lets it scale to routing between millions of distinct networks rather than just tracking individual devices on one LAN.

How devices are wired together shapes failure behavior:

![Bus, star, ring, mesh, and hybrid network topologies](assets/network-topologies.svg)

**Bus** and **ring** share one failure point (a cut cable can take the whole segment down); **star** isolates each device behind the switch, so one bad cable kills only that node — why nearly every modern LAN is physically a star.

assets.alt: Bus, star, ring, mesh, and hybrid network topologies

slides.markdown:
Networks are also classified by **scope**:

- **LAN** (Local Area Network) — one building or campus, owned end-to-end, Ethernet/Wi-Fi, low latency.
- **MAN** (Metropolitan Area Network) — a city-scale network, often fiber, connecting multiple LANs.
- **WAN** (Wide Area Network) — spans cities/countries, the internet itself is the largest WAN, typically leased lines or ISP infrastructure you don't own.

Scope drives technology choice: you'd never run raw Ethernet across a WAN — that's what routing and ISP links are for.

A **collision domain** is a set of devices that could collide if they transmit at once — a hub puts everyone in one collision domain; a switch gives **each port its own**, which is why collisions vanished once switches replaced hubs.

A **broadcast domain** is the set of devices that receive each other's broadcasts — a switch does *not* split this (it still floods broadcasts everywhere); only a router or VLANs do. Interviewers probe exactly this: switches fix collisions, not broadcast scope.

slides.sectionTitle: A home network, end to end
slides.markdown:
Put it together: every device on your home LAN is configured with a **default gateway** — the router's LAN-side IP — as the address to send anything not on the local network:

![A laptop, phone, and TV routing off-LAN traffic through a home router's default gateway](assets/home-network-gateway.svg)

The router then NATs (translates) all of that traffic onto the one public IP your ISP assigned.

assets.alt: A laptop, phone, and TV routing off-LAN traffic through a home router's default gateway

slides.subTitle: Not every gateway is a router, and vice versa
slides.markdown:
A common mistake is treating "router" and "gateway" as synonyms. **Router** names a device class — something that forwards packets between networks using IP. **Gateway** is a role: whatever a host sends off-network traffic to. Your home router plays both roles at once, which is why the terms blur.

But a gateway can be something else — an app-layer proxy translating protocols (an "API gateway," "email gateway") does no IP forwarding at all. Don't assume "gateway" implies routing hardware.
